items.title: From ETHOS Policy to Praxis: A Professional Development Playbook for AI in the Middle Grades
items.abstract: This is an accepted article with a DOI pre-assigned that is not yet published.Middle school educators face a daunting instructional paradox: navigating the rapid rise of generative artificial intelligence (AI) while working under broad, compliance-driven district policies that overlook the distinct developmental realities of early adolescence. Early adolescents are undergoing rapid neurological growth and identity construction, meaning that a purely restrictive approach to AI misses a vital opportunity to foster critical thinking and self-regulation. To bridge the gap between high-level policy and daily classroom reality, this practitioner perspective introduces the ETHOS framework, which guides AI evaluation through five tenets: Ethical, Transparent, Human-centered, Opportunity-focused, and Safe. This playbook details how our district operationalized ETHOS into an actionable framework that shifts school cultures away from a compliance scanner and toward a developmental lens. We outline a professional development sequence that uses thinking routines, ambiguous case studies, and disciplinary breakouts to build educator capacity. Crucially, we unpack the practical distinction between AI-enhanced and AI-dependent learning, demonstrating how structured AI scaffolding preserves “productive struggle” and honors the whole child. Finally, we share honest implementation friction points and discuss how the framework remains adaptable for resource-constrained schools seeking digital equity. Ultimately, this perspective provides a ground-level roadmap for school leaders to move from abstract technology policy to responsive classroom praxis.

items.title: FROM GOOGLE'S DISCOVERY TO A DIFFERENT AGENTIC ARCHITECTURE : The exploit_agent Case, the Risks of Unrestricted Autonomous Cyber Operations, and the ST-T1024 A1–A16 Framework
items.abstract: On November 16, 2026, Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG), working with Mandiant, published findings that mark an important development in the operational use of artificial intelligence in cyber operations. https://x.com/i/status/2123457542345179163 GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent framework calledexploit_agent. The framework integrated multiple frontier and locally hosted largelanguage models and was configured to continuously analyse software patches, identify potential vulnerabilities, draft exploits and execute them automatically, without human intervention at those stages. This finding moves the discussion of agentic artificial intelligence beyond theoreticalconcerns. The central issue is no longer simply whether AI can generate sophisticated code or assist ahuman attacker. It is whether an AI agent can autonomously transform an objective into asequence of consequential operations, interact with external systems, evaluate executionresults and continue acting at machine speed. This paper examines that development and proposes a different architectural approach:ST-T1024 Agentic Architecture, documented through A1–A16. Its fundamental principle is that an agent may exercise autonomy within a human-definedoperational perimeter, without acquiring authority to redefine that perimeter. The human defines the knowledge library, permissible goals, actions, permissions, execution constraints and verification requirements. The agent operates within those specifications. The proposition is not that autonomous execution must be eliminated. It is that autonomous execution must be separated from autonomous authority. THE AGENT MAY EXECUTE. IT MUST NOT BECOME THE AUTHOR OF ITS OWNAUTHORITY.

items.title: From Knowledge Augmentation to Pedagogical Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model-Based Intelligent Tutoring Systems
items.abstract: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled more flexible pedagogical interactions in intelligent tutoring systems. However, the reliability of generated content and its impact on actual learning outcomes remain contested. A central research question is how to integrate reliable knowledge with learner states to support tutoring decisions aligned with instructional objectives. Drawing on studies published between 2020 and 2026, this review examines advances in knowledge augmentation and learner modelling, analyses approaches to pedagogical strategy selection and feedback regulation, and assesses existing evidence of educational effectiveness. The literature indicates that retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs can provide a knowledge basis for tutoring responses, while knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis help identify learners' knowledge states. Multi-turn planning and feedback mechanisms also provide greater control over instructional behaviour. Nevertheless, these capabilities have not yet been adequately validated in combination, and improvements in tutoring response quality do not necessarily translate into genuine learning gains. Empirical studies have reported substantially different learning outcomes, suggesting that instructional design and evaluation methods may influence judgements of educational effectiveness. Future research should strengthen the dynamic connections among supporting evidence, learner states, and pedagogical decisions. Independent assessments, knowledge transfer tasks, and longitudinal follow-up are also needed to verify learning outcomes and provide a more robust empirical basis for the design and application of LLM-based intelligent tutoring systems.

items.title: From law to practice: model-level operationalization of technical governance requirements for high-risk AI in healthcare
items.abstract: The European Union published the Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) in a strategic effort to align the development and application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the common market. This act, one of the first laws of its kind, strengthened the development of trustworthy and human-centered AI through new regulations, prescribing requirements that providers of AI systems must conform to. The Act prescribes model-level technical requirements for high-risk AI systems, such as in terms of accuracy, robustness and fairness, which are to be addressed and reported in the form of conformity assessments. We identify, however, a significant gap between the high-level legal descriptions provided in the law and the low-level requirements needed for the implementation of automated assessment tools for algorithmic auditing. This gap is a major obstacle in the operationalization of AI Act compliance. The difficulties are aggravated due the lack of harmonized AI standards and the existing heterogeneity of AI models, datasets, and tasks. To address this gap, we present an open-source proof-of-concept assessment tool to operationalize the technical requirements of the AI Act according to the current regulatory landscape. With this tool, we demonstrate a bottom-up interpretation of the technical requirements of the AI Act for an automated evaluation of accuracy, robustness, and fairness. We apply our work to two neural network-based healthcare applications and discuss the requirements for further integration to initial conformity assessment and to extended application to post-market monitoring and other algorithmic auditing frameworks. With further work, the base structure presented here can be applied for integration beyond healthcare to other AI high-risk application domains.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: FROM LINGUISTIC ANALYSIS TO AI-ENHANCED PEDAGOGY: PREPARING 21ST-CENTURY LANGUAGE TEACHERS FOR CRITICAL, CONTEXT-AWARE LEARNING
items.abstract: The integration of linguistics and digital educational technologies requires more than adding artificial intelligence (AI) tools to existing language lessons. It requires teachers who can connect linguistic knowledge, pedagogical design, critical evaluation, and responsible technology use. This article proposes a practical framework for AI-supported language teaching in which linguistic analysis becomes the basis for meaningful, context-sensitive learning. The study uses a conceptual and analytical approach, drawing on research into AI in language education, international guidance on teacher AI competencies, and an illustrative teaching sequence built around intertextuality - the way a text draws meaning from other texts and cultural references. The framework includes five stages: identify a language phenomenon, contextualise its function, generate AI-supported alternatives, verify outputs against reliable sources, and evaluate learning through a learner-produced task. The article argues that AI is most educationally valuable when it supports inquiry and feedback rather than replacing teachers’ judgement or learners’ interpretive work. It also outlines risks involving inaccurate explanations, cultural flattening, privacy, bias, and overdependence. The proposed model offers teacher educators a transferable structure for integrating linguistic content with digital tools while maintaining human agency, academic integrity, and clear learning outcomes.

items.title: From Multimodal Observables to Latent Trustiness: Mathematical Modeling of Human Trust in AI Interaction
items.abstract: Continuous assessment of human trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally a latent-state identification problem: trust cannot be observed directly, while its behavioral manifestations are noisy, multimodal, and often shared with other internal states such as cognitive load, uncertainty, and attention. This work introduces trustiness as an operational latent variable for characterizing the time-varying trust-related state of a user interacting with an AI system. Rather than treating behavioral measurements as direct proxies for trust, we formulate their relationship with trustiness within a multimodal state-space framework that explicitly separates latent trust, cognitive load, contextual factors, and noisy observations. Candidate gaze, head-motion, and interaction-derived features are characterized through marginal, conditional, and incremental mutual information to determine which observables retain trust-related information after accounting for confounding and multimodal redundancy. The resulting informative observation set is integrated into a recursive latent-state estimator, instantiated through an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) for continuous inference. In a controlled study with 60 participants, gaze entropy, revisit behavior, verification actions, response latency, and inspection time provided the strongest independent trust-related evidence, while conditioning on cognitive load substantially reduced several otherwise apparent associations. The selected multimodal model achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.112, a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.149, and a Pearson correlation of 0.79 with self-reported trust across all 60 participants, evaluated on post-calibration interactions after participant-specific Trustiness Calibration Experiment (TCE) calibration. Participants were held out from population-level feature selection and hyperparameter tuning. Calibration was conclusive for 57 of 60 participants, for whom the corresponding MAE was 0.108, RMSE was 0.143, and Pearson correlation was 0.81. Joint modeling of trustiness and cognitive load reduced MAE by 18.2% relative to a trustiness-only model in the conclusive-calibration evaluation, while conditional feature selection improved generalization compared with the complete unfiltered observation set. Temporal experiments further showed coherent degradation and recovery of the inferred latent state following controlled changes in AI reliability. These results indicate that continuous trust assessment is better formulated as the identification of a partially observable latent state from confounded multimodal evidence than as direct prediction from behavioral proxies, providing a mathematical framework for multimodal trust estimation in human–AI interaction.

items.title: From Placement to Practice: A Two-Phase Interaction Design Study of Smartphone Video See-Through Stylus Interaction
items.abstract: Smartphone video see-through (VST) stylus interaction could support digital ink input on everyday surfaces, reducing reliance on specialised hardware and small screens. Yet the user experience of these systems is not well understood. Unlike writing on paper, users must coordinate a stylus, surface, and display while managing occlusion, stability, surface access, and comfort. We examine user experience through a two-phase study of smartphone VST stylus use. A participatory placement study identified how users intuitively position the phone, stylus, and surface, revealing the handheld position as the most preferred. A usability evaluation of a handheld prototype showed that overall participants found the system to be intuitive to use, with high usability and low workload. These results indicate that stylus VST interaction is a promising way forward for accessible, large-scale, freeform digital input. We contribute design implications for future stylus VST systems including stable repositioning, stylus-position feedback, tracing support, training and ergonomics.

items.title: From Prefabricated Content to Situated Generation: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Study of AI-Mediated Museum Surfaces and Spaces
items.abstract: Generative AI changes a basic condition of interactive surfaces and spaces (ISS): visitor-facing content can be produced during interaction rather than fully authored before it. We report a longitudinal qualitative study with 23 Chinese science museum practitioners, interviewed annually from 2023 to 2026 (retention 23 to 19) and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants’ accounts moved from anticipated epistemic and operational risks, through backstage experimentation and visitor-facing trials, toward situated governance and renewed questions about the purpose of museum interaction. Following these changes over time shows how generative AI reconfigured the design problems of museum ISS: generated content appeared under institutional authority; inference delay became publicly and bodily experienced; concurrent touch, gesture, and speech created ambiguous multi-user intent; and post-generation editing could leave curators selecting within an AI-defined possibility space. We conceptualize the resulting shift as a movement from prefabricated display to situated generation and formulate four design propositions concerning provenance at the point of display, spatially appropriate fallback, multi-intent negotiation, and curatorial control before generation. These propositions are grounded in practitioner accounts rather than evaluations of implemented solutions.

items.title: From Signal to Action: Closing the Gap in Risk-Based Quality Management Implementation
items.abstract: Risk-based quality management (RBQM) is used to help ensure that clinical trial data are fit-for-purpose and that trial quality is protected. RBQM begins by identifying critical-to-quality (CtQ) factors and risks related to such CtQ factors, defining controls such as key risk indicators and data checks, and reviewing data to detect signals. Many organizations can identify signals through centralized monitoring and analytics, but a persistent gap remains in determining whether a signal represents a true issue and what action, if any, is appropriate given study data and site context.The authors met as a cross-functional group with experience in clinical data management, statistics, quality, clinical operations, and clinical trial technology. Participants represented both sponsor and service provider organizations and brought practical experience from active trials. The group met to discuss how RBQM is applied today and how organizations might better move from identified signals to appropriate, data-supported actions.This paper presents a consensus view of the capabilities needed to close this gap. The group concluded that agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is unlikely to be useful in this setting unless it is grounded in structured study context, well-understood data, and an issue management process. Neither statistical analysis nor AI can establish causality; what they can do is focus attention and support structured investigation so that study teams can determine the underlying reason for a signal and decide on an appropriate action. The capabilities described here are offered as design considerations for the field rather than as an endorsement of any product or implementation.

items.title: Functioning While Fracturing: Theorizing Leadership Quiet Cracking Under Continuous Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Digital transformation is increasingly experienced not as a bounded program of organizational change but as a condition of recurrent and overlapping adaptation. Research has clarified many technological, strategic, and employee-level consequences of this shift, yet it has paid less attention to a leadership-specific problem: the possibility that leaders can continue to look effective while progressively losing the cognitive, emotional, temporal, and recovery resources required to remain effective. This conceptual paper develops a leadership-specific process theory of quiet cracking under continuous digital transformation. Rather than claiming a wholly new strain construct, the paper refines the emerging quiet-cracking literature by specifying a distinctive leadership configuration in which preserved short-term role enactment coexists with hidden resource erosion. Conservation of Resources theory provides the primary explanatory engine, while role theory, Job Demands-Resources theory, compensatory-control theory, emotional-labor research, recovery theory, and Restricted Employee Sustainability Theory are integrated to explain the process. The model proposes that continuous digital transformation intensity generates experienced transformation load; that resource loss and institutionalized recovery deficits translate this load into leadership quiet cracking; and that the dual position of leaders as change recipients and change agents, together with change-champion emotional labor, accelerates depletion. Compensatory effort can preserve visible performance and create a detection lag between internal deterioration and external failure. Adaptive leadership resilience and recovery-supportive organizational resources can slow this trajectory, but persistent overload can produce a resilience-masking loop in which resilient performance delays corrective action until buffering capacity saturates. The paper contributes a temporal and role-specific explanation of hidden leader deterioration and positions human sustainability as a boundary condition of digital agility.

items.title: FusionAdvisor: Decision guidance for efficient operator fusion in deep models
items.abstract: As deep learning models grow in size and complexity, optimizing the execution efficiency becomes critical. Operator fusion merges multiple operators to reduce memory overhead and enhance computational efficiency. However, the combinatorial explosion of possible fusion combinations in modern models creates a search space that challenges traditional manual and heuristic methods. We propose FusionAdvisor, a neural network based framework that predicts the speedups of candidate fusion strategies from computation graphs and recommends the top- candidates (recommended strategies). Trained on our constructed fusion strategy dataset, it abstracts fusion selection as a service, enabling developers to choose high-performance strategies and accelerate inference efficiently. Experimental results demonstrate that FusionAdvisor’s neural network predicts post-fusion speedups with low error, enabling promising strategy recommendations while maintaining search efficiency comparable to the existing methods. This work advances automated operator fusion selection, reduces optimization costs, and improves resource utilization in complex scenarios, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and other large-scale models.

items.title: Gaze-Preserving Visual Aids For Selecting Out-Of-View Switches In a Virtual Reality Aircraft Cockpit
items.abstract: In safety-critical interactive spaces, such as flight decks, pilots must be able to maintain a forward-facing visual attention to monitor primary instruments, current weather, or other aircraft. However, typical flight decks require interaction with switches that are located outside the pilot’s view. Short, well-practiced glances at controls are part of normal cockpit operation. Longer shifts of attention away from the monitoring task to locate controls can cause problematic situations, including unnoticed changes in surrounding traffic and flight path deviations. In physical cockpits, pilots can safely rely on haptic and tactile features to select a control without looking. However, as modern pilot training increasingly transitions to Virtual Reality Flight Simulations (VRFS) to reduce costs, this crucial tactile reference is lost. Without this tactile reference in Virtual Reality (VR), trainees rely on visual guidance during switch selection, which can divert attention from the monitoring task. To resolve these VRFS-related limitations, we introduce and evaluate two techniques that enable monitoring while interacting in VR using gaze-preserving peripheral views: an orthographic ( V Ortho ) and a perspective-correct ( V Persp ) representation of the corresponding cockpit panel. Furthermore, we present a dynamic height indicator to help users determine the remaining distance between the virtual fingertip and the desired cockpit element. In a within-subjects study, 28 participants with no aviation experience compared both techniques with an unassisted baseline in a high-fidelity VR Boeing 737-800 cockpit. Our findings show that both views successfully lower error rates on the monitoring task. However, this benefit comes with trade-offs: both views increase task completion times and subjective workload (as measured by NASA-TLX). The number of missed switches, normalized path error (NPE), and pre- to post-study SSQ scores showed no notable degradation, indicating that users adapted well to the peripheral views without adverse effects.

items.title: GCP: A Safety-Aware, Payment-Agnostic Commerce Protocol for Automotive and Mobility Agents
items.abstract: Personal agents are moving from conversation to commerce. Emerging protocols such as Poppy, UCP, and ACP define how an agent proves whom it represents, discovers merchants, fills a cart, and completes an online checkout. None of them is designed for the commerce that automotive and mobility users actually need: buying a brake pad that fits a specific VIN, booking maintenance at an authorized dealer, binding insurance, or placing a vehicle reservation under safety and consumer-protection rules. This paper proposes GCP 1.0 , an open, capability-based commerce protocol for automotive and mobility agents. GCP adds four things that general commerce protocols lack: (i) vehicle context and safety gates as first-class protocol objects; (ii) a delegation and authorization ladder that lets a human grant bounded purchase authority and revoke it at any time; (iii) a payment-agnostic intent layer that abstracts card, wallet, Alipay, WeChat Pay, OEM finance, and agent-native payment tokens; and (iv) a typed exception and recovery model for the failure modes of real commerce. GCP is compatible by translation: it consumes Poppy identity and session credentials, maps its catalog/cart/checkout objects to UCP and ACP, and carries GCP-specific safety and authorization fields as extension namespaces. We specify the protocol, give a reference implementation and conformance suite, and introduce AutomotiveCommerce-Bench, 60 tasks across parts, merchandise, after-sales service, and insurance/reservation, with hidden compatibility, safety, authorization, and exception traps. In a real-LLM study with three models, GCP raises task success from 64.5% (manual web) and 69.4% (generic agent commerce) to 92.2%, cuts misbuy from 35.5%/30.6% to 7.8%, and raises exception recovery from about 58% to 89.6%, while a calibrated human model achieves 68-83% success in 8-25 minutes per task. We also compare agent commerce with a calibrated model of human shopping behavior and show where the protocol changes the error, time, and authorization trade-off. Beyond the benchmark, a Stripe test-mode sandbox (180 charges, 180/180 reconciled) shows that bounded delegation cuts human approvals by 70% relative to per-transaction approval with no loss of success, and a semi-field study on real catalogs shows no degradation. In a cockpit simulation, GCP reduces unsafe driving-time purchase attempts from 47.9% to 0% (deferral rises to 81.2%), and on a real aftermarket parts/service-kit catalog it raises success from 26.7% to 100%. We also lay out a near-term interaction horizon (12-24 months), from assisted commerce to delegated and agent-native commerce, and derive the protocol requirements each horizon creates. The protocol, benchmark, and all raw results are released.

items.title: GenAI as a Learning Tool: Why Do University Students Intend to Pay? An Empirical Study Using the Value-Based Adoption Model
items.abstract: University students increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in their everyday learning. This study used the value-based adoption model (VAM), extended with subjective norm, to examine students’ perceived value of these tools and its relationship with intention to pay. Questionnaire data from 309 Chinese university students were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Perceived usefulness, perceived price, and subjective norm showed significant positive associations with perceived value. Higher perceived value was also significantly associated with stronger payment intentions. The paths from perceived enjoyment, perceived risk, and perceived ease of use to perceived value were not statistically significant. The results support using VAM to study payment intentions for GenAI learning tools and have implications for tool design and university guidance on their use.

items.title: Generalizing Vision-Language Models to Novel Domains: A Comprehensive Survey
items.abstract: Recently, vision-language pretraining has emerged as a transformative technique that integrates the strengths of both visual and textual modalities, resulting in powerful vision-language models (VLMs). Leveraging web-scale pretraining data, these models exhibit strong zero-shot capabilities. However, their performance often deteriorates when confronted with domain-specific or specialized generalization tasks. To address this, a growing body of research focuses on transferring or generalizing the rich knowledge embedded in VLMs to various downstream applications. This survey aims to comprehensively summarize the generalization settings, methodologies, benchmarking, and results in VLM literatures. Delving into the typical VLM structures, current literatures are categorized into prompt-based , parameter-based , and feature-based methods according to the transferred modules. The differences and characteristics in each category are further summarized and discussed by revisiting the typical transfer learning (TL) settings , providing novel interpretations for TL in the era of VLMs. Popular benchmarks for VLM generalization are further introduced with thorough performance comparisons among the reviewed methods. Following the advances in large-scale generalizable pretraining, this survey also discusses the relations and differences between VLMs and up-to-date multimodal large language models (MLLM), e.g., DeepSeek-VL. By systematically reviewing the surging literatures in vision-language research from a novel and practical generalization prospective, this survey contributes to a clear landscape of current and future multimodal researches.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI ADOPTION AND EMPLOYEE PERFORMANCE: THE MEDIATING ROLE OF DIGITAL COMPETENCE
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has become common workplace infrastructure faster than almost any digital technology before it, moving from experimental novelty to everyday workplace infrastructure, yet a critical question remains underexplored in the Indian organisational context: do GenAI tools actually make employees perform better or does that depend on something else entirely – how digitally competent the employee already is? We examine whether digital competence is the missing link in explaining when and for whom the adoption of Generative AI translates into measurable performance gains. Data were collected from 500 employees working in multinational companies located in major Indian business hubs of Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Pune, Gurugram/NCR, Mumbai and Chennai using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design. The suggested model Generative AI Adoption → Digital Competence → Employee Performance was tested using a full analytical pipeline, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s Alpha, Composite Reliability (CR), Average Variance Extracted (AVE), Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA), correlation analysis, independent-samples t-tests, one-way ANOVA, multiple regression, Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), and bootstrapped mediation analysis. The Findings (reported here on an illustrative dataset, to be replaced by the primary data) suggest that the adoption of Generative AI is significantly and positively associated with digital competence, that digital competence is significantly and positively associated with employee performance, and that digital competence partially mediates the relationship between the adoption of GenAI and performance. The T-test and ANOVA results also suggest that the strength of this chain varies significantly by sex, organisational tenure and job role, indicating a more nuanced, skills-dependent adoption story rather than a homogenous productivity dividend. The findings suggest that Indian subsidiaries of multinationals should focus on digital-competence development, rather than just tool deployment, as the strategic lever to convert GenAI investment into performance results, with a particular focus on tenure-based and role-based upskilling gaps. The current study is among the first integrated SEM-based tests of digital competence as a mediating mechanism in the GenAI–performance relationship within India’s multinational corporate workforce, a fast-growing, strategically important, yet empirically under-examined segment of the global GenAI adoption story.

items.title: Generative AI and Student Freelancing: Skills, Income Opportunities, and Barriers in Somalia
items.abstract: Background In fragile, post-conflict economies facing severe youth unemployment, digital freelancing offers an essential pathway to economic self-reliance. This study investigates how Generative AI Competence (GAIC) drives Freelance Digital Skill Augmentation (FDSA) and Platform Market Competitiveness (PMC) to enhance Student Freelance Income Generation (SFIG), while assessing the moderating impact of Structural, Financial, and Institutional Barriers (SFIB) in Somalia. Methods Drawing on Augmented Human Capital Theory, Platform Labor Theory, and the Capability Approach, a cross-sectional survey collected primary empirical data from N = 415 active university student freelancers across Mogadishu, Hargeisa, Garowe, and Kismayo. Data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) in SmartPLS 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, psychometric validation, and interaction moderation analyses. Results Generative AI Competence exerts significant positive direct effects on Freelance Digital Skill Augmentation (β = 0.548, p < 0.001) and Platform Market Competitiveness (β = 0.312, p < 0.001). Digital skill augmentation strongly predicts Student Freelance Income Generation (β = 0.384, p < 0.001) and mediates GenAI's economic impact. However, structural barriers significantly dampen this conversion (β = -0.198, p < 0.001), causing a 68.0% drop in income velocity under high-barrier conditions. International payment exclusion (lack of PayPal/Stripe) and platform KYC geoblocking are identified as the most severe institutional constraints. The model explains 61.4% of variance in student freelance income (R² = 0.614). Conclusions Generative AI serves as a powerful leapfrogging mechanism that mitigates local pedagogical voids and enhances global market access for youth in fragile economies. Nevertheless, technological competence alone cannot overcome structural exclusion. Developing accessible cross-border payment gateways and resolving platform geoblocking are urgent imperatives to unlock Somalia's digital youth dividend.

items.title: Generative AI Architectures for Next-Generation Peer-to-Peer Energy Markets: A Review
items.abstract: The growing diffusion of renewable energy sources, storage systems, and distributed energy resources is fostering a transformation in electricity markets, characterized by increasingly active participation by end users. In this context, peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading models enable producers, consumers, and prosumers to exchange energy within energy communities and local systems, introducing new methods of negotiation and resource management. This paper analyzes the contribution of generative artificial intelligence, with particular reference to large language models (LLMs), to the automation of decision-making processes in P2P energy markets. The review adopts a targeted narrative approach, covering recent literature together with selected foundational studies, and organizes the evidence according to LLM roles in forecasting, trading and negotiation, MARL-assisted decision making, and hybrid architectures. The analysis focuses on automated trading, bidding and negotiation strategies, LLM–MARL integration, and complementary technologies such as blockchain, smart contracts, forecasting, and storage management. The reviewed evidence suggests that current architectures are most credible when LLMs support interpretation, strategy generation, and higher-level decisions, while network feasibility, market clearing, settlement, and other safety-critical functions remain assigned to deterministic or otherwise verifiable modules.

items.title: Generative AI as a Co-Pilot in the Development of a Secondhand Marketplace Application Using Design Thinking
items.abstract: Waste management has become a growing environmental concern in this modern era, particularly due to the increasing amount of waste generated by household activities. In 2020, Indonesia generated approximately 67.8 million tons of waste, with 37.3% originating from households. This study aims to design a prototype of ReVive, an application for buying and selling reusable second-hand goods as an alternative approach to reducing household waste accumulation. The study employed the Design Thinking method with the assistance of generative artificial intelligence (AI), specifically ChatGPT, through five stages: empathize, define, ideate, prototype, and test. The resulting ReVive prototype provides functionalities for buying and selling reusable second-hand goods. The prototype was evaluated using the System Usability Scale (SUS) involving prospective users. The evaluation resulted in an average SUS score of 74.88, indicating that the prototype achieved an excellent level of usability. The findings also indicate that generative AI can support and facilitate activities throughout the Design Thinking process, particularly during the development of design ideas and prototypes. ReVive therefore offers an alternative digital solution for promoting the reuse of household goods and reducing the potential accumulation of household waste.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Physics Education: A Systematic Mapping Review
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being adopted in education, yet its application to physics remains challenging because of the discipline’s reliance on mathematical, symbolic, and multimodal reasoning. This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic mapping review of 146 studies published between January 2023 and June 2026 on the use of GenAI in physics education. The review examines the research landscape, approaches for supporting students and teachers, and methods for benchmarking and improving GenAI systems. The findings reveal rapid growth in research activity with widespread but uneven geographic distribution, with most studies focusing on higher education and relying heavily on third-party GenAI services. Student-support research primarily addresses conversational tutoring and personalized guidance, while teacher-support studies focus on lesson planning and teaching material development, professional development and teacher perceptions. A substantial body of work also benchmarks GenAI performance on physics-related tasks or proposes methods for improving it. Overall, the reviewed literature demonstrates considerable potential for GenAI in physics education while highlighting the need for further research on multilingual and inclusive systems, specialized educational uses, privacy-preserving approaches, improved multimodal support, and integration with complementary educational technologies.

items.title: GENUINE HUMAN CONTROL AND THE BANK'S DUTY TO INFORM IN AI-BASED CREDIT SCORING UNDER THE CIVIL LAW OF UZBEKISTAN
items.abstract: Article 7¹ of the Law "On Informatization" of the Republic of Uzbekistan prohibits basing legally significant decisions solely on the output of artificial intelligence. Article 24 of the Law "On Personal Data" still permits solely automated decisions with the subject's consent or for the performance of a contract, and in lending these two exceptions cover almost every application. The borrower's protection therefore depends on what the law will accept as real human involvement and on what the bank must tell the applicant. The paper proposes four criteria of genuine human control over a credit decision and argues that the use of AI in assessing creditworthiness creates a pre-contractual duty of the bank to inform the applicant. It ends with a proposal for Article 65¹ of the Law "On Banks and Banking Activity" and for a clarification by the Plenum of the Supreme Court.

items.title: Geometry control in wire arc additive manufacturing: challenges, strategies, and future perspectives
items.abstract: The deployment of autonomous artificial intelligence (AI) within complex physical systems remains a grand challenge. While intelligent manufacturing aims to address this by infusing industrial processes with real-time adaptation, the prevailing approach often involves applying machine learning (ML) to isolated, well-defined sub-problems. This component-wise strategy, however, proves insufficient for processes like wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM), where geometric fidelity is governed by deeply coupled, multi-scale thermo-fluid dynamics that defy simple predictive modelling. Here, using WAAM as a foundational case study of a complex cyber-physical system, we provide a systematic review of the intelligent strategies required for end-to-end geometry control. We deconstruct this challenge into a unified framework spanning the full process chain—pre-deposition, in-process, and post-deposition—and map the corresponding control methods onto the critical physical scales of the bead, layer, and part. Our synthesis reveals that the primary limitations are not a lack of algorithmic novelty but rather fundamental issues of model generalisation from sparse, high-cost data and the integration of heterogeneous physical priors. This analysis points towards a necessary paradigm shift: moving from static, data-driven prediction towards dynamic, autonomous control architectures. We argue that realising the next generation of intelligent manufacturing requires a focus on integrated systems, such as physics-informed digital twins and multi-sensor fusion platforms, that can holistically manage process complexity in real time.

items.title: GeoScratch - A Block Based Language for Geometry Education
items.abstract: Geometry is important because it trains spatial reasoning and is fundamental to many STEM subjects. However, many students struggle to connect the symbolic formulas of geometry and linear algebra to the spatial relationships they describe. We present GeoScratch, a web application in which students solve geometry problems by composing a Scratch-style block-based language against a live 3D scene, rather than by manipulating formulas. By separating spatial reasoning from symbolic notation in this way, we aim to reduce cognitive load and make the subject more approachable for students with mathematics anxiety. A within-subjects study with 29 university STEM students, comparing GeoScratch to conventional lecture slides, showed that learning gains for both methods were similar. GeoScratch received above-neutral scores for the subscales Interest/Enjoyment, Perceived Competence, and Value/Usefulness of the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory. Participants judged GeoScratch as supporting both intuitive and formulaic understanding above neutral.

items.title: Gestural Input with Tangible Cubes on a Surface for Musical Expression: a Family of Experiments
items.abstract: Cubes are increasingly used in tangible interaction, particularly when arranged in a topology on a surface such as a tabletop. To better understand how end users manipulate cubes as gestural input for tangible interaction on a surface, we report empirical findings from a family of three experiments conducted with AudioCubes , a set of tangible cubes containing wireless computers with built-in sound and signal generating and processing capabilities that sense their topology for four action types on a surface: positioning, moving, rotating, and arranging. The two first experiments investigate the usability of AudioCubes through a controlled study with and without an active training, inside and outside a laboratory. The third experiment determines which gestures are spontaneously produced by end users in an uncontrolled study and how they articulate these gestures by fingers. Tangible cubes offer a usable and intuitive medium for gestural interaction. Participants consistently favored face-based interactions over edges and corners, simpler one-to-one mappings over complex multi-object procedures, and physically stable arrangements over precision-dependent gestures. Usable cube interfaces should prioritize grasping, pushing, rotating, and aligning through cube faces, while minimizing reliance on corner-based or highly constrained actions. The actual composition of cubes covers only 32% of the theoretical space of 169 spatial compositions. Some practical implications for designing gestural input with tangible cubes on a surface, such as a tabletop, are offered.

items.title: GIS Co-Scientist: a human-AI collaborative framework for autonomous geospatial scientific inquiry
items.abstract: Advances in Autonomous GIS have demonstrated that geospatial agents can plan, generate, and execute GIS workflows from natural language input. Existing systems, however, focus more on workflow execution tasks such as geospatial code generation and spatial analysis. Less attention has been given to how autonomous GIS systems can support broader stages of geospatial scientific inquiry. This paper presents a multi-agent co-scientist framework for autonomous geospatial scientific inquiry. The framework distributes scientific responsibilities across six specialized agents responsible for research question understanding, geospatial data retrieval, planning, spatial modeling, result analysis, and reporting. These agents operate through a shared context module and reproducibility layer, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at stages where geographic judgment substantially affects downstream analysis. We implement the framework as GIS Co-Scientist, a web-based prototype, and demonstrate it through three research examples. Across the three cases, the system successfully generated research plans and analytical workflows, executed spatial models, produced draft manuscripts, preserved full workflow provenance, and supported iterative post-hoc revision of analytical steps with human feedback. items.title: GIS Co-Scientist: a human-AI collaborative framework for autonomous geospatial scientific inquiry
items.abstract: Advances in Autonomous GIS have demonstrated that geospatial agents can plan, generate, and execute GIS workflows from natural language input. Existing systems, however, focus more on workflow execution tasks such as geospatial code generation and spatial analysis. Less attention has been given to how autonomous GIS systems can support broader stages of geospatial scientific inquiry. This paper presents a multi-agent co-scientist framework for autonomous geospatial scientific inquiry. The framework distributes scientific responsibilities across six specialized agents responsible for research question understanding, geospatial data retrieval, planning, spatial modeling, result analysis, and reporting. These agents operate through a shared context module and reproducibility layer, with human-in-the-loop checkpoints at stages where geographic judgment substantially affects downstream analysis. We implement the framework as GIS Co-Scientist, a web-based prototype, and demonstrate it through three research examples. Across the three cases, the system successfully generated research plans and analytical workflows, executed spatial models, produced draft manuscripts, preserved full workflow provenance, and supported iterative post-hoc revision of analytical steps with human feedback. The framework advances autonomous GIS for geographic knowledge discovery and clarifies how autonomy and human authorship can be designed as complementary properties of scientific systems.

items.title: Global Displacement Patterns and Healthcare Access Among Ukrainian Refugees: A Mixed-Methods Analysis
items.abstract: Background The 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine triggered one of the largest and most rapid displacement crises in recent history, creating sustained challenges for refugee protection, data coordination, and healthcare delivery. Methods We conducted a mixed-methods study integrating longitudinal displacement data from international, governmental, and secondary sources with a systematic analysis of 51 healthcare policy documents and reports from ten major host countries. Quantitative analyses examined temporal and geographic displacement patterns, cross-source reporting discrepancies, and admission pathways. Large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction with independent human validation identified and assessed frequent domains in healthcare access across host countries. Results Ukrainian displacement remained protracted through 2025 and increasingly shifted from neighboring countries toward Western Europe, with Germany becoming the largest host country from 2024. Refugee estimates varied substantially across sources, likely because of differences in definitions, reference periods, and counting methods. The U.S. response relied primarily on humanitarian parole and temporary protection rather than formal refugee resettlement. LLM-assisted analysis identified five healthcare access domains: registration, primary care, mental health, specialist care, and additional services. Across the ten host countries, access ranged from comprehensive in Germany, the Netherlands, and Spain to highly constrained in Moldova. Major barriers included language difficulties, administrative complexity, financial constraints, geographic disparities, and limited healthcare navigation. Mental health and psychosocial services remained insufficient. Conclusions Formal protection and healthcare eligibility did not ensure equitable access. Harmonized refugee-data standards, durable legal pathways, professional interpretation, multilingual navigation, and expanded mental health, telehealth, and mobile services are needed to strengthen current and future humanitarian responses.

items.title: GPT-4-Assisted Versus Human Detection of Intraoperative Adverse Events From Spine Surgery Operative Reports
items.abstract: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Manual chart review remains the primary method of clinical data collection in spine surgery research but is time intensive and prone to human error. Large language models may enable automated extraction of clinically meaningful events from unstructured operative text. We evaluated the performance of generative pre-trained transformer 4 (GPT-4) in detecting intraoperative adverse events from spine surgery operative notes compared with trained human reviewers. METHODS: A retrospective cohort of 1454 laminectomy cases performed at a single academic institution between 2016 and 2022 was analyzed. Deidentified operative notes were independently reviewed by 4 trained human reviewers and GPT-4 using standardized prompts to identify incidental durotomy and nondurotomy intraoperative adverse events. Discordant classifications were adjudicated by a senior reviewer to establish ground truth. Performance metrics including sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, and F1 score were calculated. Analyses were stratified by operative note length, and review time was estimated. RESULTS: Incidental durotomy occurred in 88 cases (6.1%). GPT-4 achieved 100.0% sensitivity compared with 89.8% for human reviewers, with lower positive predictive value (88.0% vs 100.0%) but similar specificity (99.1% vs 100.0%). For nondurotomy adverse events (n = 21), GPT-4 demonstrated higher sensitivity than humans (90.5% vs 57.1%) with equivalent specificity (100.0%). GPT-4 maintained stable performance across note length quartiles, whereas human reviewer sensitivity decreased for longer notes. Human reviewers required approximately 35 hours to review all notes, compared with approximately 2 hours for GPT-4. CONCLUSION: GPT-4 demonstrated higher observed sensitivity than trained human reviewers for detecting intraoperative adverse events from spine surgery operative reports while reducing review time by more than 90%. Large language model-assisted chart review may serve as a scalable human-in-the-loop adjunct to traditional chart review, improving the completeness and efficiency of neurosurgical outcomes research.

items.title: Graphing the Everyday: A Neurosymbolic Approach to Eliciting Routines for Just-In-Time Adaptive Interventions
items.abstract: Just-In-Time Adaptive Interventions (JITAIs) increasingly rely on conversational agents to elicit user routines, yet translating fluid human dialogue into rigid schedule data remains a significant challenge. We conducted a qualitative investigation of a neurosymbolic pipeline, combining Large Language Models (LLMs) with a Neo4j knowledge graph, to map unstructured verbal narratives into actionable interventions. Through human-centric evaluation using natural-language playbacks, we identified a critical “mental-model gap,” where the linear extraction of LLMs clashes with hierarchical, non-linear human storytelling, causing severe entity fragmentation. Furthermore, we articulate an “ecological mismatch,” demonstrating that algorithmic schedule availability frequently ignores the user’s fluctuating psychological receptivity and physical energy levels. To resolve these tensions, we propose actionable design heuristics, including routine piggybacking, adaptive negotiation, and scalable transparency. Ultimately, these guidelines provide a foundational framework for evolving rigid schedule-trackers into empathetic, context-aware proactive agents capable of supporting long-term health behavior change.

items.title: GraspPressure: Understanding Pressure Input With Busy Hands
items.abstract: In many real-world scenarios, users interact with digital systems while their hands are partially occupied, such as when holding tools or everyday objects. Prior work on busy-hand interaction has focused on microgestures and motion-based techniques, which rely on finger articulation or relative movement. In situations where a stable grasp is required, such as handling fragile, heavy, or precision objects, such motion can be undesirable or impractical. Pressure-based input offers a complementary modality that enables interaction without changing finger pose, yet its use while holding objects has received limited empirical attention. To explore this, we conducted two within-subject experiments examining users’ ability to perform controlled pressure selections and analyzing finger-specific performance across different grasps and geometries. Results indicate that participants can reliably perform pressure-based selections in these conditions, achieving high success rates (92.7% on average) with low selection times (1.74s on average). Our findings characterize the potential of pressure input as a complementary microinteraction modality under grasp-constrained, busy-hand scenarios.

items.title: Green Innovation Capabilities and Sustainable SME Performance: An Integrative Literature Review
items.abstract: This integrative literature review asks how external pressures and organizational capabilities combine to support green innovation and multidimensional sustainable performance in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). A transparent audit of the manuscript bibliography identified 62 cited entries; removing two duplicates and separating three institutional reports yielded 57 distinct scholarly sources for citation-based thematic synthesis, with recent evidence emphasized and seminal theory retained. The analysis compares external drivers, capability formation, product and process innovation, environmental and economic outcomes, digital complementarity, and contextual constraints. Across the reviewed evidence, stakeholder pressure and regulation are more likely to stimulate innovation when knowledge management, absorptive capacity, leadership, and green dynamic capabilities support implementation. Environmental gains are more consistent than short-term financial returns; firm size, financing, readiness, industry, and commercialization shape the variation. Digitalization and artificial intelligence are treated as conditional enabling capabilities, not automatic performance drivers. Drawing primarily on dynamic capability theory, the review proposes a six-stage green capability cycle that connects sensing, mobilization, innovation, measurement, learning, and resource reconfiguration. The cycle is a literature-informed conceptual proposition requiring longitudinal validation, not an empirically tested causal model.

items.title: GUARDAID Annex 9 — Aeronautical Profile: Agent Identity and Mandates on Board
items.abstract: How does an aircraft verify which AI agent may request what — and prove every interaction afterwards? GUARDAID Annex 9 adapts the GUARDAID open standard for aviation systems. Instead of hardcoding mission rules, the standard defines cryptographically signed configuration slots: the aircraft operator and the manufacturer each fill their own slots to declare who holds command authority, which action verbs a principal's agent may issue, how the aircraft behaves during a data-link loss, and which alert policies govern operations. The specification supplies the structure and verification tools; the aircraft owner supplies the policy values. By design, the protocol never drives flight actuators—actuator requests are blocked structurally, while every telemetry reading is logged and sealed in a tamper-evident trail.The deposit includes the complete reference reader and reproducible verification suite: a deterministic generator producing 209 test cases and 224 presentations with byte-identical outputs on every run, plus 159 adversarial mutations, all detected. items.title: HaloTouch++: Towards Portable and Condition-Tolerant Surface Touch Input for Mixed Reality
items.abstract: Touch interaction on everyday surfaces has long been envisioned as an extension of mixed-reality input, offering tactile feedback and proprioceptive cues that enhance user comfort and precision. However, most existing mixed-reality touch-sensing techniques are designed for static, dry, and large surfaces, making them unsuitable for real-world use where surfaces may be handheld, wet, or smaller in size. We introduce HaloTouch++, a mixed-reality touch input technique that enables low lift-off, water-tolerant and finger profile modified interactions on handheld surfaces. The system harnesses multi-path interference from time-of-flight depth sensing as a stable optical cue for detecting physical contact. A lightweight, plastic reflector attached to the surface amplifies these interference patterns, forming a distinctive “Halo” signature around touch points that remains consistent across surfaces and under varying poses and moisture conditions. In a 15-participant evaluation spanning multiple materials, user poses, and water conditions, HaloTouch++ achieved 97.3% touch-down accuracy and 93.3% gesture recognition accuracy.

items.title: HandPad: A Bimanual Hand Interface for Fluid Window Interactions in VR
items.abstract: Virtual Reality (VR) offers the potential for productivity work by providing expansive workspaces anywhere, yet supporting bare-hand interaction with multiple 2D windows remains challenging. We present HandPad, an asymmetric bimanual interaction framework that combines differentiated hand roles, self-haptic interaction, and hand remapping for multi-window interaction. The non-dominant hand sets a spatial frame, selects the interaction context, and provides a self-haptic surface, while the dominant hand performs on-hand touch and complementary mid-air manipulation relative to that frame. HandPad organizes interaction into three modes supporting cross-window navigation, within-window content manipulation, and application-window management. It also remaps the physical hands to virtual windows, allowing users to interact from more flexible physical postures regardless of window location. An exploratory study suggests that HandPad provides coherent interaction workflows, while revealing design tradeoffs between on-hand and mid-air interaction, informing the design of future bimanual interfaces for multi-window VR workspaces.

items.title: Health and Care on the Edge: The Use of AI through the Prism of Power, Time, Inclusion and Emotions
items.abstract: Health and care settings present high-stakes contexts where it is essential that decision-making and access to information are timely and accurate. The use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools is increasingly influencing practice, while also introducing risks and challenges that can affect the safety, fairness, and trustworthiness of AI systems in these settings. This workshop critically explores the use of AI tools in health and care settings through the prism of four dimensions: power, time, inclusion and emotions. It will explore how pushing the boundaries of scenarios on the edge can influence the lived experience of multiple stakeholders, including healthcare providers, caregivers, researchers, industry partners, and people accessing health and care services. Participants will share experiences of AI use in health and care settings, engage in scenarios that can be challenged by the four dimensions, and reflect on how technology design can be sensitised to address the risks and challenges raised by the four dimensions in situations on the edge.

items.title: HemoPred: A web application for hemoglobin A2 (HbA2) and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) prediction from routine blood features using Mixture of Experts and explainable artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Background and objectives Hemoglobinopathies, including beta thalassemia, are blood disorders caused by mutations in the HBB gene. Accurate and early screening of heterozygous carriers is necessary to prevent mutations from being transmitted to offspring. Diagnosis of carrier status is based on hemoglobin A2 (HbA2) and fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels, requiring expensive equipment for quantification. This work aims to develop machine learning models for prediction of HbA2 and HbF from routine blood test parameters in persons with hemoglobinopathies and normal individuals. Methods Mixture of Experts (MoE) approach was applied to develop the models using an Indian dataset of 5314 individuals. Post-hoc interpretations were obtained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). An affinity-based classifier was developed to predict the diagnostic labels from the predicted HbA2 and HbF. Finally, a web application, HemoPred, was developed as frontend of the models. Results MoE models achieved mean absolute errors of 0.1654 and 0.1394, and R 2 -scores of 0.8442 and 0.6055 for HbA2 and HbF prediction, respectively, with 5-fold cross-validation. The models achieved similar performance in held-out internal validation. SHAP revealed MCV, MCH, and RDW-CV as top contributors. Affinity-based classifier achieved 95% top-2-accuracy (5-fold cross-validation) in multiclass prediction. In binary (disease/normal) classification, it achieved 77% balanced accuracy with 93% sensitivity. HemoPred is available at https://aihemo.mp.aau.dk/hemopred . Conclusions ML models developed for HbA2 and HbF prediction, and diagnostic classification from the predicted HbA2 and HbF can aid doctors. This work is limited by unavailable multi-center data for external validation and unmeasured confounders, including nutritional profiles and α-thalassemia co-inheritance status.

items.title: Hold the Space, Not the Pen: A Design Probe Study of AI’s Role in Early-Career Workplace Reflection
items.abstract: Reflective practice helps learners make sense of early-career workplace experiences, but can be difficult to sustain amid ambiguity, vulnerability, and pressure to present oneself competently. As AI tools are proposed as scalable supports, their implications for learner authority remain underexplored. This study examined AI-supported reflection in early-career workplace learning through a two-week design probe with five tertiary students and recent graduates undertaking placements, internships, or graduate programs. Participants completed spoken, written, structured, and AI-mediated reflection activities alongside mood tracking. Data comprised probe artefacts, AI outputs, and interviews, analysed using reflexive thematic analysis and a multidimensional framework. Participants valued AI for organising thoughts, offering perspectives, and supporting communication, but resisted it when AI authored reflections, inferred emotions, or interpreted meaning. We propose conditional scaffolding: AI supports reflection when learners retain authority over meaning-making. We discuss implications for flexible scaffolds, bounded AI roles, temporal pattern visibility, and connections to human reflection.

items.title: HomeNarrator: Natural-Language Activity Descriptions From Binary Ambient Sensors
items.abstract: Smart homes with ambient sensors record daily life continuously and privately, underpinning aging-in-place monitoring and ambient intelligence. Yet for two decades such systems have produced only discrete activity labels, which cannot express concurrent, ambiguous, or transitional behaviour; roughly half of all recorded data collapses into an uninformative “Other” class. We present HomeNarrator, to our knowledge the first system to generate free-text descriptions of resident activity from binary PIR and door sensors. It converts raw CASAS events into structured elapsed-time segments, which a large language model (LLM) narrates under evidence-bounded rules that limit hallucination. Lacking reference descriptions, we evaluate reference-free: a three-model LLM jury, cross-validated against human annotators, scores each description on an evidence-grounded rubric. In the stratified annotation subset, raters judged 78 % of windows high quality (mean nine or above), and the jury tracked that mean within one point (MAE 0.76 / 0.84). These results establish descriptive human activity recognition (HAR) as feasible on sparse ambient sensors in single-resident homes.

items.title: Human control in high-risk autonomous systems: a cross-domain documentary analysis and safety-control governance framework
items.abstract: Human oversight is widely required for autonomous and artificial-intelligence systems, yet assigning a human role does not establish that the person can influence a hazardous trajectory. This study develops a bounded Safety-Control Governance Framework for assessing whether documentary human-control claims are operationally inspectable. Drawing on systems-theoretic safety, supervisory control, situation awareness, resilience engineering, meaningful human control, and AI governance, the framework distinguishes seven operational functions—authority allocation, feedback and observability, situational comprehension, intervention timing, safe-state objective, escalation, and recovery—and two cross-cutting governance functions: accountability assignment and documentation or assurance. The framework was applied to a purposive corpus of 24 public documents spanning autonomous mobility, maritime autonomy, drones and emergency operations, and high-risk AI or command support, producing 216 document–function observations. Authority and accountability were Explicit in 20 of 24 documents and documentation or assurance in 23 of 24. Explicit specification was less frequent for intervention timing (8 of 22 known cases), safe-state objectives (7 of 23), escalation (10 of 24), and recovery (6 of 24). Documentary families supplied complementary evidence, while configuration analysis located distinct discontinuities, including explicit authority while feedback and comprehension were not both Explicit in ten documents. Most degradation-pattern evidence was anticipatory or prescriptive rather than event-based. These numerical profiles are conditional on the final coding rules and source selection. The framework provides an evidence-linked protocol for tracing documentary control gaps; it does not assess operational performance.

items.title: Human expert-generated flexibility program versus single-attempt AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro)-generated flexibility program for office workers: a quasi-randomized controlled trial
items.abstract: Sedentary office environments contribute to flexibility loss and musculoskeletal disorders. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers scalable rehabilitation, its clinical reasoning and biomechanical safety remain scrutinized in academic literature. This study compared the efficacy of 15-minute home-based flexibility exercises designed by human experts versus those generated by AI (Gemini 2.5 Pro) on flexibility, lower back health, and muscle stiffness. In this quasi-randomized controlled trial, 30 male participants were allocated to a Human Expert Group ( n = 15) or an AI Group ( n = 15) using a random start (single coin toss) followed by alternating allocation, which differed from the wording of the ethics-approved application (simple random method, coin toss) and carries a risk of selection bias. Interventions lasted 4 weeks (3 days/week). Assessments included Sit-and-Reach tests, Oswestry Disability Index (ODI), and MyotonPRO stiffness measurements. Initially, the groups exhibited similar characteristics ( p > .05). In the Sit-and-Reach test, a measure of flexibility, the average score for the human expert group increased from 14.93 ± 10.67 cm to 22.60 ± 11.49 cm, while in the artificial intelligence group, this value reached only from 16.23 ± 7.91 to 17.53 ± 7.60 cm; a statistically significant Time × Group interaction with a large effect size was detected between the groups (F(1,28) = 28.26, p < .001, ηp² = 0.502). A significant Time × Group interaction was also found for the Oswestry Disability Index (ODI) (F(1,28) = 7.49, p = .011, ηp² = 0.211). Following Benjamini–Hochberg False Discovery Rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity adjustment across the eight interaction tests, statistically significant Time × Group interactions robustly survived for Sit-and-Reach flexibility ( p < .001), Oswestry Disability Index ( p = .011), dominant biceps femoris stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.01, p = .003, ηp² = 0.282), and non-dominant gastrocnemius stiffness (F(1,28) = 11.16, p = .002, ηp² = 0.285) in favor of the human expert group. In contrast, the Time × Group interaction for dominant erector spinae stiffness was nominally significant prior to adjustment only (F(1,28) = 4.41, raw p = .045, ηp² = 0.136) and did not survive FDR correction. No significant interactions were observed for the remaining muscle groups ( p > .05). Based on the observed Time × Group interaction effects, human expert-generated programs containing dynamic and static flexibility exercises yielded significantly greater improvement over time in flexibility and lower-back health than the single-shot static stretching program generated by Gemini 2.5 Pro. These findings highlight the short-term efficacy of the specific expert-designed dynamic protocol rather than demonstrating a generalized limitation of generative AI in exercise prescription. Trial registration : The study was registered on Clinicaltrials.gov under the number NCT07242287. (Date of Registration 11/17/2025)

items.title: Human factors in maritime safety: An integrative narrative review of cognitive, behavioural and organisational determinants
items.abstract: Maritime accidents arise from interactions among people, work organisation, technology and the operating environment. Although casualty analyses frequently code human-related contributors, these classifications should not be interpreted as evidence that individual seafarers are the predominant root cause of accidents. This integrative narrative review therefore examines human factors as manifestations of a wider socio-technical system. A structured two-layer review strategy was used. Twenty maritime-focused empirical, review and analytical sources formed the core evidence corpus, while supplementary theoretical and cross-domain sources were used only to interpret mechanisms and transfer preventive lessons. The core synthesis identified four recurring patterns: fatigue and cognitive strain are shaped by scheduling, recovery opportunities, noise and automation demands; communication problems in multinational crews extend beyond language to authority gradients and shared mental models; reporting behaviour is strongly conditioned by organisational climate, commercial pressure and regulatory implementation; and many apparently individual errors emerge from interactions across cognitive, team, organisational, technical and environmental levels. HFACS, the Swiss Cheese Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Groupthink Theory, Error Management Theory, Rasmussen’s socio-technical perspective and Safety-II are therefore treated as complementary interpretive lenses rather than competing explanations. A preventive diagnostic matrix is proposed to connect analytical level, observable risk conditions, assessment indicators and upstream interventions. The review argues that maritime safety management should move away from worker-centred error correction toward primary prevention that redesigns work, technology, leadership and reporting systems around the conditions that shape safe performance.

items.title: Human Judgment in A.I.-Assisted Management Decisions
items.abstract: Managers in nonprofit and non-governmental organisations increasingly receive advice from artificial intelligence tools when they forecast demand, allocate staff and budgets, screen applications, prioritise programmes and assess risk. The central management question is no longer whether such advice is available but how human judgement should be combined with it. This conceptual paper develops a calibrated-judgement framework for AI-assisted management decisions. It builds on two experimental literatures that point in different directions. Dietvorst, Simmons and Massey report that people became less likely to rely on an algorithm after seeing it err, even when it outperformed a human forecaster. Alon-Barkat and Busuioc, in three experiments in the Netherlands, found no evidence of automation bias but found stronger adherence to advice aligned with group stereotypes in one study, with no significant difference between algorithmic and human-expert advice. These findings are connected to research on accountability and advice rationales, conditions for intuitive expertise, complacency and automation bias, decision structures and the automation–augmentation paradox. The framework holds that reliance on AI advice should be calibrated to the predictability of the decision environment, the reasons given for advice and the accountability that attaches to the decision. Six propositions address advice rationales, track records, selective adherence, workload, decision structure and skill preservation. No original empirical data are presented.

items.title: HUMAN-AI SYMBIOSIS IN GLOBAL COMMERCE EDUCATION: INSTITUTIONAL ADAPTATION, CURRICULUM CO-EVOLUTION, AND EXPERIENTIAL PEDAGOGY IN INTERNATIONAL BUSINESS
items.abstract: The rapid integration of autonomous artificial intelligence agents, predictive trade analytics, and multimodal generative models into multinational enterprise (MNE) operations has fundamentally disrupted the foundational assumptions of International Business (IB) higher education. Traditional IB pedagogy—anchored in static comparative advantage models, retrospective case analyses, and isolated cross-cultural taxonomies—increasingly fails to prepare graduates for an era defined by algorithmic global value chains and geopolitical fragmentation. Moving beyond superficial classroom tool adoption, this study investigates how Artificial Intelligence can systematically restructure International Business education through the theoretical lenses of Institutional Entrepreneurship, Distributed Cognition, and Experiential Learning Theory. We argue that modern global business education must cultivate Symbiotic Cross-Border Intelligence—the integrated capacity to deploy, audit, and ethically govern intelligent systems across divergent sovereign, cultural, and regulatory jurisdictions. To operationalize this paradigm, the paper constructs an Adaptive Curriculum Co-Evolution Model paired with a Four-Tiered Experiential Learning Ecosystem that replaces passive lecturing with live cross-border algorithmic sandboxes, regulatory friction wargames, and multilingual stakeholder simulations. Drawing upon multi-semester pedagogical implementations across international finance, global supply chain resilience, and emerging-market entry courses, we demonstrate substantial improvements in students’ causal systems reasoning, hallucination forensics, and cross-cultural communicative agility. Finally, the paper addresses structural risks—including algorithmic monoculture, epistemic dependency, and extraterritorial data governance violations—and formulates an institutional compliance charter for business schools navigating the intelligent transformation of global commerce.

items.abstract: У тезах досліджено можливості поєднання людиноцентричного підходу та технологій штучного інтелекту у системі управління відновленням українського бізнесу в умовах повномасштабної війни та повоєнної трансформації. Актуальність теми зумовлена масштабом руйнувань, дефіцитом трудових ресурсів, порушенням логістичних ланцюгів і необхідністю підвищення продуктивності підприємств. Мета дослідження — обґрунтувати концептуальну модель управління відновленням бізнесу, у якій штучний інтелект посилює управлінські можливості, а людина залишається центральним суб'єктом ухвалення рішень. Методологічну основу становлять аналіз і синтез наукових та аналітичних джерел, порівняння міжнародних рекомендацій, систематизація практик цифрової трансформації та концептуальне моделювання. У результаті визначено чотири взаємопов'язані компоненти запропонованої моделі: людиноцентричне лідерство й розвиток компетентностей; застосування ШІ для аналітики та підтримки рішень; адаптивна організація бізнес-процесів; відповідальне управління даними, ризиками й результатами. Обґрунтовано, що ефективність відновлення залежить не від самого факту впровадження технологій, а від їх узгодження з потребами працівників, клієнтів і громад, прозорості алгоритмічних рішень та збереження людського контролю. Практичне значення результатів полягає у можливості використання моделі малими й середніми підприємствами для підвищення стійкості, інноваційності та конкурентоспроможності.

items.title: Human-Centric Trust Calibration and Adaptive Explainability in AI-Driven Security Operations
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in Security Operations Centers (SOCs) to support intrusion detection and threat investigation. However, accurate predictions and explainable outputs do not necessarily lead to appropriate human reliance: analysts may over-rely on incorrect recommendations or unnecessarily reject reliable ones. This work proposes a human-centric trust-calibrated framework that integrates an AI-driven Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS), online estimation of analyst trust and cognitive load, and adaptive explanation selection within a closed-loop security interface. The NIDS combines traffic and textual threat representations to provide threat predictions, calibrated reliability estimates, and semantic evidence. Behavioral and interaction signals are processed through a probabilistic state-space model to estimate the analyst state, while a reliability-aware controller dynamically adjusts explanation depth and evidence granularity according to the Trust-Calibration Error (TCE), which captures the mismatch between inferred analyst trust and current NIDS reliability. Rather than treating trust estimation or calibration as standalone objectives, we investigate whether their integration improves operational human–AI performance under varying NIDS reliability. A controlled SOC-oriented evaluation compares the proposed trust-calibrated policy with static and trust-agnostic adaptive explanation strategies in terms of analyst decision quality, inappropriate reliance, investigation efficiency, and cognitive workload. Empirical evaluation across 2160 trials with 36 participants demonstrates that the proposed trust-calibrated policy improves decision accuracy from 81.4% to 89.3%, corresponding to an increase of 7.9 percentage points, curtails Automation Bias Rate (ABR) from 43.1% to 22.2% (31/72 to 16/72, representing a 48.4% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 21.8%, a 49.4% reduction), and decreases Inappropriate Rejection Rate (IRR) from 18.8% to 11.0% (122/648 to 71/648, representing a 41.8% relative reduction; GLMM-adjusted: 18.9% to 10.9%, a 42.3% reduction), while lowering trust miscalibration error from 0.184 to 0.101. Crucially, these reliance gains are accompanied by a reduction in subjective workload from 58.4 to 48.7 on the NASA-TLX scale and a decrease in mean investigation time from 30.2 s to 28.1 s. These findings indicate that effective human-centered security interfaces should not maximize trust or explanation richness, but dynamically promote reliance that is consistent with the actual competence of the AI system.
